cells: I04 · Text doesn't meet the 4.5:1 contrast ratio
Text falls below the WCAG 1.4.3 minimum contrast against its background (4.5:1 for body text; 3:1 for 18pt+ or 14pt-bold).
Users with low vision, color blindness, or who view the site in bright sunlight can't read the text. This is one of the most commonly-reported barriers in user testing.
All text on the affected pages clears 4.5:1 (body) or 3:1 (large) against its background, verified in DevTools or WebAIM.

B. Put the text on its own surface
Change the background, or place the text on a solid panel or scrim, so contrast stops depending on whatever sits behind it.

cells: I14 · Images don't announce text to screen readers
One or more elements have no alt attribute (or have alt="" when the image is informative). Screen readers announce "image" with no context, so the information the image conveys is unreachable.
Blind, low-vision, and screen-reader users get a broken version of the page, the image's content is silently dropped.
Every on the affected pages has either a non-empty alt attribute that describes its purpose, or alt="" explicitly when decorative.

Scan #1 of https://example.org/. 5 page(s) crawled. Browser-rendered. Viewport 1280x800. Engines: axe-core (AA), Alfa. Scanned April 22, 2026.
Component framework and assistive technology tested:, (add before sharing)
Instances, one row per occurrence found

• For each affected image, decide what the image conveys. If it conveys information, write alt text that describes the *meaning*, not the appearance ("Acme logo", not "blue square with letters"). • If the image is purely decorative (a divider, a stock photo with no semantic role), set alt="" explicitly so screen readers skip it cleanly. • Update the CMS field or the template so the alt attribute is always present, even when empty.
With a screen reader running (VoiceOver: Cmd+F5 on macOS; NVDA: Ctrl+Alt+N on Windows), tab to each affected image. It should announce meaningful text or be skipped entirely if marked decorative.
Approaches shared for context, not prescribed. Use what fits the codebase, as long as the acceptance criteria hold.
A. Describe the image's meaning in its alt attribute
Decide what each image conveys where it sits, and write that meaning into alt. Describe the purpose, not the appearance: "Acme logo", not "blue square with letters".
The same file can need different alt text on different pages. A logo that is also a link to the home page describes the destination, not the picture.
B. Mark it decorative and carry the meaning in nearby text
If the image only repeats adjacent text or is purely ornamental, set alt="" so screen readers skip it cleanly, and make sure the surrounding text carries the information.
alt="" on the only source of some information hides it completely, and an image with alt="" inside a link leaves that link with no name at all.

cells: I15 · Form controls have no programmatic label
Input controls (text fields, checkboxes, selects) lack a <label for=…>, aria-label, or aria-labelledby. Screen readers announce them as "edit text" or similar with no purpose.
Without a programmatic label, users with screen readers or voice input can't tell what a field is for or address it by name. Form completion becomes guess-and-check.
Every input on the affected forms has a <label for=…>, an aria-label, or an aria-labelledby that names the field.

Component framework and assistive technology tested:, (add before sharing)
Instances, one row per occurrence found
• For each input, add a
Tab into each form field. The screen reader should announce the field's purpose immediately. Click the visible label; the focus should move into the matching input (proves the for/id pairing).
Approaches shared for context, not prescribed. Use what fits the codebase, as long as the acceptance criteria hold.
A. Associate a visible label element
Give the control a <label for="..."> matching its id, or wrap the control in the label.
The for value must match the input's id exactly, and placeholder text is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types.
B. Name the control for assistive technology only
Use aria-label where a visible label would genuinely be redundant, such as a search field sitting immediately beside a Search button.
A control with no visible label is harder for everyone, not just screen- reader users. Keep this for the few cases where surrounding context is unambiguous.
C. Reference an existing visible string
Use aria-labelledby to name the control from text already displayed, such as a table row or section heading.
Ids must be unique, and when several are referenced the reading order follows the order listed, not the order on screen.

cells: I16 · The page has no top-level heading

No level-one heading was found in the rendered page. Headings that are present may be hidden with display: none, or the text that looks like a heading may be a div, span, or button carrying a typography class that only changes font size. Styling text to look large does not make it a heading, and nothing hidden with display: none reaches the accessibility tree.

Screen reader users navigate by heading. Without an outline they cannot jump to a section, cannot get a sense of what the page contains, and cannot confirm which page they are on, they are left reading the page line by line. Sighted users with cognitive disabilities lose the same structural cue.

The page exposes a logical heading structure with exactly one h1 and a clear h1 to h6 outline with no skipped levels, and no heading is hidden with display:none, visibility:hidden, or zero dimensions.

Approaches shared for context, not prescribed. Use what fits the codebase, as long as the acceptance criteria hold.
A. Promote the visible text into real headings via the component's tag prop

Delete the headings hidden with display:none and let the components that already look like headings render as real ones. Component libraries usually expose this directly, such as a tag prop on a title component.
Where the thing that looks like a section label is an interactive control, keep the control and put a real heading above it rather than turning a button into a heading.
B. Use standard heading tags, with a screen-reader-only class where needed

Replace the typography wrappers with h1 to h3. Where a heading genuinely should not be seen, use the framework's visually-hidden class rather than display:none, which hides it from assistive technology as well as from the screen.
Native heading tags bring their own margins and can override component-library spacing, so check the layout after the swap.

cells: I21 · Top-level content isn't inside a landmark
Page content appears outside any landmark element (no <main>, <nav>, <header>, <footer>, or [role="region"]). Screen-reader users can't jump to the page's main content via landmark navigation.
Screen-reader users navigate by pulling up a list of landmarks and jumping between sections (VoiceOver: VO+U → Landmarks; NVDA: D key). Content outside landmarks is invisible in that list.
Every page has a <main> wrapping its primary content, plus semantic landmarks for nav, header, and footer.

Instances, one row per occurrence found

• Wrap the page's primary content in a <main> element. There should be exactly one per page. • Wrap the nav in <nav>, the page header in <header>, and the footer in <footer>. These are HTML5 landmarks by default.
Run a screen reader's landmark navigation. The main content should be reachable in one keystroke (VoiceOver: VO+U then Landmarks; NVDA: D key).

Approaches shared for context, not prescribed. Use what fits the codebase, as long as the acceptance criteria hold.
A. Wrap the content in landmark elements
Put the page's regions inside header, nav, main, aside and footer so every meaningful block sits in a landmark.
The rule flags content that falls between landmarks, so partial adoption still fails: anything meaningful has to end up inside one.
B. Apply ARIA landmark roles where the tag cannot change
Add role="main", role="navigation" and similar to existing containers when the element itself is fixed by a component library.
Prefer the native elements. A role on the wrong container, such as one that wraps both the nav and the content, is more misleading than no role at all.

cells: I29 · Links have no accessible name
One or more <a> elements have no visible text, no aria-label, and no aria-labelledby. Screen readers either skip them or announce "link" with no destination context.
Screen reader users navigate by pulling up a list of links; an unnamed link is invisible in that list. Keyboard users also can't tell where the link goes from the focus indicator alone.
Every <a> on the affected pages has either visible text or an aria-label / aria-labelledby that describes the destination.

A name is not yet a purpose: "Read more" repeated twenty times passes this rule and still fails SC 2.4.4 in context.
B. Name it for assistive technology only
Add an aria-label, or a visually hidden span inside the link using the framework's screen-reader-only class.
aria-label replaces the visible text entirely, which breaks voice control when the spoken name no longer matches what is on screen. Where visible text exists, extend it with a hidden span instead.
C. Point at text that is already on the page
When the link's purpose is written next to it, such as a card title, reference that element with aria-labelledby.
The referenced id must exist and be unique. A duplicated id silently names the link after the wrong element.

axe flags missing alt on img / area / input[type=image] and unlabelled SVGs; the image-of-text VLM separately flags pictures that are really text.
Whether the alt text that IS present is a meaningful equivalent, and the decorative-vs-informative call, needs a human.

Confirm the transcript is accurate and equivalent. Video-only (silent video) can't be detected from the DOM, still a manual check.

Confirm an audio description or full text alternative for prerecorded video.
Confirm live audio in synchronized media has real-time captions.

axe checks list, table-header, definition-list, required-ARIA-children and heading-structure markup on the rendered DOM.
Relationships conveyed only visually (grouped fields, columns, emphasis that implies meaning) need a human to confirm they're also programmatic.

The visual probe screenshots the page and asks a local vision model whether the visual reading order matches the DOM/source order (CSS can reorder content so screen readers hear a different sequence).
Confirm the model's call by tabbing/reading with a screen reader. Subtle reorderings and content below the fold still need a human, and the probe only runs when a local vision model is available.
Read instructions for reliance on shape/size/location/sound alone ("click the round button to the right"), judgement only a human can make.
Confirm content isn't locked to portrait or landscape (rotate the device / check for orientation-locking CSS).
axe validates that any autocomplete tokens used are valid.
Confirm autocomplete IS present on fields collecting the user's own info (name, email, address), missing autocomplete isn't auto-detected.
axe flags links distinguished from surrounding text by colour alone (a narrow heuristic).

The visual probe measures actual playback advancement and flags audible audio longer than three seconds when no native or explicitly associated custom control is detected. Autoplay markup alone is not flagged.
Confirm every audible autoplay source can be paused, stopped, or volume controlled independently; test custom controls and browser autoplay policy.
axe measures text/background contrast on the rendered DOM against the 4.5:1 (3:1 large-text) thresholds.
Text baked into images, hover/focus/disabled states, and text over gradients or photos need a human to check.
The responsive probe zooms to a 200% proxy viewport and flags text that clips or overflows its container.
Confirm no loss of content or function across the full zoom range in your target browsers.
OCR + a local vision model judge whether each image is really rendered text rather than a photo/diagram.
Confirm flagged images aren't the allowed exceptions (logos, or text that's essential to a particular presentation).
The responsive probe loads each page at 320 CSS px and flags horizontal scrolling / overflow.
Confirm no content or functionality is lost in the reflowed view (some loss can pass the geometry check but still fail in use).
Check that UI component boundaries (inputs, buttons, focus rings) and meaningful graphics meet 3:1. No reliable automated rule exists yet.
The responsive probe injects the WCAG text-spacing override CSS (line-height 1.5, etc.) and flags clipping/overlap.
Confirm no text is cut off or overlapping with the spacing applied.
For tooltips/popovers triggered by hover/focus, confirm they're dismissable, hoverable, and persistent.
axe flags some keyboard-inaccessible patterns; the keyboard probe confirms focus can move through the page.
Confirm every control (menus, custom widgets, drag handles) is fully operable by keyboard, the deepest part of this SC is manual.

The keyboard probe emits a review lead only when the same observable element resists repeated Tab and Shift+Tab exit attempts. It suppresses normal focus wrapping, small focus cycles, modal containment, and opaque iframe or closed-shadow focus.

Reproduce every lead and test components that appear after interaction. Confirm whether arrow keys, Escape, a close control, or a documented non-standard command lets the user leave before recording a failure.
If single-character shortcuts exist, confirm they can be turned off, remapped, or are active only on focus.
For any time limit, confirm it can be turned off, adjusted, or extended.
The visual probe measures actual playback advancement for visible video longer than five seconds without a detected control. It also records <marquee> as an expert-review lead.
CSS animations, auto-advancing carousels, and auto-updating regions aren't auto-detected, confirm any content that moves >5s can be paused, stopped, or hidden.
Confirm nothing flashes more than three times per second. Flash analysis is not implemented.
axe checks for a skip link, landmark regions, and a heading structure that lets users bypass repeated content.
Confirm the skip link actually moves focus and works with the keyboard.
axe checks that every page has a non-empty <title>.
Confirm the title is descriptive and distinguishes the page (a light human check).

Tab through the whole page and confirm the focus order preserves meaning and operability, the order can break without a positive tabindex (e.g. CSS-reordered columns), which still needs a human.
axe flags empty/unnamed links; the semantic LLM judges whether the link text plus its context conveys where it goes.
Confirm the LLM's borderline calls ("read more", icon links), it flags strong leads, not verdicts.
Confirm at least two ways to find pages (nav + search, or sitemap), except for steps in a process.
axe flags empty headings / unlabelled controls; the semantic LLM judges whether each heading actually describes the content it introduces.
Confirm the LLM's borderline heading calls, and check that form-control LABELS are descriptive, label descriptiveness is not yet AI-assisted.
axe has limited checks for suppressed focus indicators.
Tab the whole page and confirm a clearly visible focus indicator on every interactive element, largely manual.
The live-page focus probe focuses each element and flags any whose centre is covered by a position:fixed/sticky overlay (the classic "focus hidden behind the sticky header" failure).
Confirm partial-overlap cases the centre-point check can miss, and tab through interactively, overlays that appear only after a click still need a human.
For any multipoint/path gesture (swipe, pinch), confirm a single-pointer alternative exists.
Confirm actions fire on the up-event and can be aborted (no critical action on down-press).
axe flags controls whose accessible name doesn't contain the visible label text (label-content-name-mismatch).
Confirm the visible text is fully contained in the accessible name for voice-control users.
If a function is triggered by device motion (shake/tilt), confirm a UI alternative and a way to disable motion actuation.
For any drag operation (sliders, reorder, kanban), confirm a single-pointer alternative (tap/click) exists.
axe checks interactive targets are at least 24x24 CSS px (with spacing).
Confirm the inline / essential / equivalent-control exceptions are genuinely met for any flagged small targets.
axe checks <html> has a present and valid lang attribute.
Confirm the declared language actually matches the page's main content.
axe validates lang attributes that are present on parts of the page.
Detecting foreign-language passages that are *missing* a lang attribute needs a human reader.
Confirm moving focus to a control doesn't trigger an unexpected context change (auto-submit, new window).
Confirm changing a setting (select, checkbox) doesn't auto-trigger a context change without warning.
Confirm navigation repeated across pages stays in the same relative order. A cross-page embedding analyzer is on the roadmap.
Confirm components with the same function are labelled consistently across pages. A cross-page analyzer is on the roadmap.
Confirm help mechanisms (contact, self-help) appear in the same relative order on every page that has them.
Submit forms with invalid data and confirm errors are identified in text. Requires interaction the crawler doesn't perform.
axe checks a programmatic label exists; the semantic LLM judges whether each control's label/instructions are sufficient to know what to enter.
Confirm the LLM's sufficiency calls, and test real form submissions, error-time instructions (SC 3.3.x) still need a human.
Trigger validation errors and confirm the page suggests how to fix them.
For legal/financial/data submissions, confirm reversal, checking, or confirmation is available.
In multi-step flows, confirm previously-entered info is auto-populated or selectable rather than re-typed.

Manually test each in-scope sign-in and MFA step. Custom widgets' state changes (expanded, selected, checked) need a screen reader to confirm they're announced.
axe checks for some live-region / role=status markup.
Confirm dynamic updates (added-to-cart, validation, search counts) are actually announced, needs screen-reader testing.
